Atharvaveda
------------------------------------------
The most ancient and basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म् are known as ‘Vedas.’ Derived from the root ‘vid’ (= to know), they represent a vast body of religio-spiritual knowledge transmitted orally from generation to generation over the millennia. Hindu tradition ascribes to the sage कृष्ण-द्वैपायन, better known as व्यास, the systematization and editing of the vast Vedic literature with a view to preserving it for the posterity. He is said to have divided the वेदस् into four parts and taught it to his four chief disciples viz., पैल, वैशम्पायन, जैमिनि and सुमन्तु. These four वेदस् have been well-known as Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāma-veda and Atharvaveda (vide महाभारत, Ādiparva 60.5; Bhāgavata 12.6.50).
The Atharvaveda, the last in the series, has also been called by several other names: Atharvaṇaveda, अथर्वाङ्गिरस, Āṅgirasa, Bhṛgvaṅgirasa, भृगु-vistara, Brahmaveda, Bhaiṣajyaveda and Kṣattraveda.
The word ‘Atharvan,’ probably derived from ‘athar,’ an obsolete word for fire, might mean ‘the priest of fire.’ So, अथर्वन् may be the name of an ancient sage who ‘brought down fire from हेअवेन्’ and started the sacrificial rites here.
In the Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य्, he is descri-bed as a son of ब्रह्मा, the Creator, who introduced fire-rituals with सोम and other materials. He is identified with अङ्गिरस् and also called अथर्वाङ्गिरस. It is also possible that the ṛṣis of the clans of अथर्वन्, अङ्गिरस्, भृगु, अथर्वाङ्गिरस and ब्रह्मन् were the ‘draṣṭāras’ of this Veda, i.e., the sages to whom the various hymns of this Veda were revealed. Hence the other names of this Veda.
The title ‘Brahmaveda’ could have been derived from the fact that it was related to the priest ब्रह्मा, the fourth of the four priests, the other three being hotā, अध्वर्यु and udgātā, connected with the first three वेदस् in that order. In a more general sense it can also mean the Veda that helps in the attainment of ब्रह्मन्.
The two names ‘Bhaiṣajyaveda’ and ‘Kṣattraveda’ have obviously been derived from the subject matter of the Veda which contains quite a bit of material on ‘bhaiṣajya’ (medicines and treatment) and ‘kṣattra’ (the warrior-class known as the kṣattriyas).
The Atharvaveda has some special features because of which it stands a little apart from the other three वेदस्, especi-ally the Ṛgveda. It deals more with the things here and now, than the hereafter, and, the sacrifices which are a means to it. Major portion of this Veda is concerned with diseases and their cure, rites for prolonging life, rites for fulfilling one’s desires, building construction, trade and commerce, statecraft, penances and propitiatory rites and ब्लच्क्-मगिच्, though high philosophical ideas, much nearer to the thought pattern of the उपनिषद्स्, are also to be found. Even the literary style is more sophisticated. Hence some scholars believe that this work had not been admitted into the comity of Vedic literature for a long time. It was perhaps considered as a ‘scripture of the masses,’ not fit enough for admission into the ‘elite-group;’ and its sheer popularity might have forced the leaders of the society into admitting it as the fourth Veda and give its priests also an honourable place in sacrifices.
For the same reasons, it is opined that this Veda is chronologically posterior to the other three वेदस्. Some modern scholars like C. V. Vaidya (vide History of Vedic Literature, p. 156) assign to it, the period 3000 to 2500 B. C. But, Vedic chronology is a rather hazardous subject and it is very difficult to fix the periods precisely.
From the ancient times, nine शाखास् or branches of the Atharvaveda (Saṁhitā) are known to have existed. However, only two of them are extant: पिप्पलाद and शौनक. Of these, it is the latter that is available in a complete form.
This Veda is divided into four ‘prapāṭhakas,’ comprising 20 ‘kāṇḍas.’ Each kāṇḍa is again sub-divided into ‘sūktas’ and these sūktas, into ‘mantras.’ The details are as follows:
Prapāṭhakas Kāṇḍas Sūktas Mantras
I 1 to 7 433 2030
II 8 to 12 45 1573
III 13 to 18 43 1063
IV 19 & 20 215 1411

This gives us 6077 mantras in 736 sūktas spread over 20 kāṇḍas in 4 prapāṭhakas. However, due to the different methods adopted in grouping or classi-fying, the number of sūktas given by various scholars have varied from 598 to 759. But there is no difference in the number of the mantras.
The last kāṇḍa, i.e., the 20th, has borrowed heavily (to the tune of 90%) from the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā. It is opined that the kāṇdas 19 and 20, sometimes termed ‘Khilakāṇḍa,’ are later additions to this Veda.
Coming to the subject matter of the Saṁhitā of this Veda, we find that there is no systematic division of the same in the first twelve kāṇḍas. The last two again, deal with miscellaneous topics. A brief summary of the contents may now be attempted, under eight subject headings:
1. Bhaiṣajya Sūktas :
These sūktas which deal with disea-ses, their causes and cures, show a remarkable insight into the subject of health sciences. That is why this Veda is considered to be the precursor of Āyurveda or the Science of health and longevity. Sometimes, Āyurveda is listed as an उपवेद or subsidiary of the Atharvaveda. These sūktas contain many prayers for health and longevity. The various names of the parts of the body given here bespeak of an intimate knowledge of human ana-tomy. Several diseases like fever, leuco-derma, leprosy, jaundice, diabetes, dropsy, skin disorders, troubles of the ear, nose and throat, fracture of bones, diseases of the heart and tuberculosis, are mentioned and cures indicated. These diseases are caused by germs, violation of the laws of nature, anger of deities and malevolent spirits and sins committed previously. Apart from medicines and physical remedies, use of chants and charms was also in plenty. A deep knowledge of the herbs and their various medicinal properties can be inferred from many of the mantras.
2. आयुष्य Sūktas :
These sūktas contain supplications for longevity and are to be uttered on auspicious occasions like चौल (tonsure), उपनयन (investiture with the sacred thread), गोदान (gifting of cows) and so on. The desire to live the full span of life, viz., 100 years, is often expressed. One of the sūktas (kāṇḍa 17) prescribes the wearing of the ‘rakṣāsūtra’ (‘thread of protection’) on the body to attain longevity.
3. Pauṣṭika Sūktas :
Puṣṭi means worldly progress and welfare. These sūktas generally contain prayers for the blessings of deities like the Maruts, Parjanya and others so that there can be good rains and crops, and, works like होउसे-building or agriculture or trade flourish well.
4. Ābhicārika Sūktas :
If the Pauṣṭika Sūktas are intended to bring prosperity, the Ābhicāraka Sūktas are aimed at destroying or harming enemies who obstruct our progress or try to destroy us. This is said to be achieved by pleasing or appeasing certain deities or spirits and getting one’s wishes fulfilled through them. This technique is called ‘yātu’ or ‘kṛtyā.’ The number of such sūktas is rather large. Destruction of one’s enemies including the lovers of one’s spouse, annihilation of evil spirits, mesmerizing others through whom one can get one’s desires fulfilled—these are some of the topics dealt with in these sūktas. The word ‘kṛṣṇendrajāla’ is sometimes used to indicate the type of ब्लच्क्-मगिच् rites depicted here. As opposed to this, the auspicious rites described in the Pauṣṭika Sūktas are called ‘śuklendrajāla.’
5. प्रायश्चित्त Sūktas :
These are concerned mainly with expiatory rites to offset the evil effects that may come as a result of non-perfor-mance or wrong performance of religious rites. Omens foreboding evil and the rites necessary to combat them are also described.
6. Strīkarma Sūktas :
These sūktas deal mainly with marri-age, love and allied topics. Rites that help in regaining the lost love of one’s spouse are also described.
7. Rājakarma Sūktas :
This section gives an account of the political system that obtained during those days. The king used to be elected by the people. National and social problems used to be discussed by or decided in a ‘samiti’, a parliament of the people. The Rājapurohita (Chief Priest of the State) had an enviable place in the affairs of the State. Prayers for victory in war and hymns expressing devotion to the Motherland given here are highly poetic and moving.
8. Brahmaṇya Sūktas :
These sūktas unfold the nature of ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute. The philosophical ideas given here form a link between those of the Ṛgveda and of the उपनिषद्स्.
God, the Absolute, is designated here by various names such as Kāla, स्कम्भ, उच्छिष्ट and Vrātya which are rather peculiar to this Veda. From him the whole universe emerges and in him is it established. He is the lord of the whole च्रेअतिओन्. The universe has evolved out of him, because he willed it thus (vide 19.53.8). The sun is a symbol of his power and is called ‘Rohita,’ the ‘Red-One’. He is identi-fied with God himself. This Absolute is also identified with the आत्मन्.
The word ‘Vrātya’ found in this section has nothing to do with the people who had been without Vedic sacraments, the sense in which the word has been used in the धर्मशास्त्रस्. Here it repre-sents ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute.
The Atharvaveda Saṁhitā gives us an interesting picture of the society of its times. The land in which the people lived extended from गान्धार (Afghanistan) to Magadha and अङ्ग (Bihar and Bengal). The वर्ण system had been well established. The first three vaṛṇas were called ‘Āryas’ and the fourth as ‘Śūdras.’ But people lived in harmony. Kings were powerful. Trade and commerce were prosperous though agriculture was their main stay. There are hints to show that the ब्राह्मणस् were powerful and had sometimes to face the wrath of the क्षत्त्रिय kings. The cow was highly venerated and गोदान (gift of cows) was considered highly meritorious. There are references to the राजसूय sacrifice and wars among kings. The institute of मर्रिअगे was very similar to that of the Ṛgvedic times; so also the obsequial rites.
No Āraṇyaka of the Atharvaveda has come to light so far. Only one ब्राह्मण has been discovered, the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa.
The three well-known Upaniṣads—the Praśna, the Muṇḍaka and the Māṇḍūkya—belong to this Veda.
(For details see under the respective titles.)
In conclusion it can be said that the अथर्ववेद forms an important landmark in Vedic literature.

Atharvaśikhā Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a small Upaniṣad belonging to the Atharvaveda. It is in prose. It is divided into three sections containing twenty mantras.
Three sages—Pippalāda, अङ्गिरस् and Sanatkumāra—approach the venerable Atharvaṇa and seek instructions from him on meditation. Atharvaṇa teaches them meditation on Om or प्रणव which is the best symbol for ब्रह्मन्, both in its higher and in its lower aspects. The three parts of Om, viz., a, u and m, as also the last unseen part, are described as representing the various aspects and levels of च्रेअतिओन्. For instance, a represents the earth, the Ṛgveda, ब्रह्मा and the deities known as वसुस्. It also represents the गायत्री metre and the गार्हपत्य fire. Similarly, u stands for the intervening space between the earth and हेअवेन्, the Yajurveda, रुद्र, and the eleven subsi-diary deities also called Rudras, as also the triṣṭubh metre and the dakṣiṇa fire. The syllable m indicates हेअवेन्, the Sāmaveda, विष्णु, the deities called Ādityas, the जगती metre and the आहवनीय fire. The last unseen half-syllable (‘ardhamātrā’) is the symbol of the Atharvaveda, the ‘saṁvartaka’ fire that destroys च्रेअतिओन् at the end of the cycle and the deities called Maruts.
Meditation on this प्रणव leads to लिबेरतिओन् from rebirth.

Ātharvaṇa-jyotiṣa
(‘Science of heavenly bodies, belonging to the ’)
------------------------------------------
Jyotiṣa or अस्त्रोनोम्य् is one of the six वेदाङ्गस् or subsidiary sciences that help us to understand the वेदस्. Since performance of sacrifices was the most important aspect of the Vedic religion and it was related to different periods of the year as also time and the position of the स्तर्स्, a separate science called ‘Jyotiṣa’ was evolved in course of time. Each of the four वेदस् developed its own Jyotiṣa.
The work Ātharvaṇa-jyotiṣa as extant today comprises 162 verses and may be a recast of an earlier work. It is generally assigned to the 2nd cent. B. C. It deals with मुहूर्त (a particular division of time), karaṇa (an astrological division of day), योग (leading star of a lunar aste-rism; a variable division of time), tithi (lunar day) and vāra (day of the week). It is said to fall outside the Vedic period but before the period of the सिद्धान्त चलेन्दर् which divides the zodiac into twelve rāśis or signs. It adopts a scheme of नक्षत्र अस्त्रोलोग्य्. It forms nine groups of three nakṣatras (asterisms) each, the total being 27. Information is provided at length as to what should be done or not to be done on the presence of the nine groups and their constituents.
See also JYOTIṢA.

Atharvan
------------------------------------------
The word is probably derived from ‘athar,’ an obsolete word for fire, and hence means a priest connected with the worship of fire. According to Vedic म्य्थोलोग्य्, अथर्वन् was son of ब्रह्मा, the Creator. He first brought down fire from हेअवेन् and offered सोम into it with the recitation of appropriate mantras learnt from his ड़थेर्. He is sometimes considered as the propagator of the fourth Veda which is hence called the Atharvaveda or the Atharvaṇaveda. His wife was Śānti, the daughter of कर्दम प्रजापति. He is sometimes identified with अङ्गिरस्, called Atharvāṅgiras, and is considered as the ड़थेर् of अग्नि, the fire-god.
This word, as also the word Atharvāṅgiras, is sometimes used to indicate the descendants of this sage.
The word अथर्वन् also refers to the hymns of the Atharvaveda.

Atharvaśira Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This Upaniṣad, as its very name indicates, belongs to the Atharvaveda. It is also called Atharvaśīrṣa Upaniṣad. It is classified under minor उपनिषद्स् and consists of seven sections in prose.
The first section describes how the gods went to the svargaloka (heaven) and asked रुद्र who he was. He replied that He was the primeval Supreme Person and that whatever existed was He. The gods then, realizing His supremacy, praised Him with their hands raised in adoration. The second and the third sections contain their hymns of praise. The fourth section defines and amplifies some of the epithets used in praising रुद्र. The fifth section contains some well-known ṛks of the Ṛgveda and a description of the parts (a, u, m) of Om or प्रणव, including their symbology. The sixth section also contains some well-known mantras of the Ṛgveda and Kṛṣṇa यजुर्वेद. The last section is a eulogy of the results one gets by a study of this Upaniṣad.
